title: Cannabis Anatomy: Roots, Stems, Leaves, Nodes and Flowers

content.overview: Cannabis anatomy provides the structural vocabulary needed to understand cultivation. Roots, stems, leaves, nodes, internodes, meristems, and reproductive structures each contribute different functions and create observable evidence about plant development.

vocabulary.definition: A region of actively dividing plant cells that produces new growth.
A point on a stem where leaves, branches, or reproductive structures arise.
The stem segment located between two neighboring nodes.
A reproductive shoot system bearing flowers and associated structures.

sections.title: Roots and the root-shoot connection
sections.body: Roots anchor the plant, acquire water and mineral nutrients, and interact continuously with the aerial shoot through vascular transport. Root condition can therefore influence leaf expansion, water status, nutrient symptoms, and whole-plant vigor.

sections.title: Stems, nodes and meristems organize growth
sections.body: Stems support leaves and reproductive structures while carrying water, minerals, and assimilates. Nodes and meristems define where branches and flowers can develop, so recognizing them is essential for propagation and canopy-management decisions.

sections.title: Leaves connect light, gas exchange and water loss
sections.body: Leaves are major sites of photosynthesis and gas exchange. Their form and orientation affect light interception while stomatal activity links carbon dioxide uptake with water loss to the atmosphere.

sections.title: Reproductive structures change the cultivation context
sections.body: As plants enter reproductive development, floral structures become increasingly important for sex identification, pollination risk, maturity assessment, and harvest planning. Structural observations should be interpreted together with developmental stage.

workedExamples: When identifying a cutting site, locate a healthy stem segment with suitable nodes rather than choosing tissue only by total length.
When evaluating maturity, compare actual floral development at representative positions instead of using plant height as a proxy.
commonMistakes: Calling every stem junction a meristem.
Treating roots as separate from above-ground plant behavior.
Using leaf shape alone to identify cultivar or sex.
content.practicalApplication: During plant inspection, label the major organs and record node spacing, branching pattern, leaf condition, root observations where available, and reproductive structures. Use these structural notes as context for later environmental and diagnostic measurements.
content.summary: Cannabis cultivation becomes easier to reason about when plant structures are identified correctly. Roots, stems, leaves, nodes, meristems, and flowers form an integrated system whose structure changes through development.
